---
title: "The Covariance Matrix"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "The Covariance Matrix"
  description-meta: "Why the sample covariance matrix fails on a realistic universe, and the four things to do about it: fewer assets, a factor structure, shrinkage, or a robust estimator."
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(PortfolioAnalytics)
library(knitr)
```

Suppose we have an equity sleeve to fill. There are one hundred and twenty-three
names in the eligible universe, thirty-one model years of monthly returns are
available, and we want the combination of them with the lowest risk. That is the
most modest request anyone makes of a portfolio optimizer: no view, no forecast,
no tilt, just the low-volatility end of the frontier of @sec-09-mean-variance-theory.

We will not get it. Not because the data are poor and not because the optimizer is
badly written, but because the object it requires cannot be estimated from the
data available. @michaud1989 named the consequence and @chopra1993 priced it, but
the failure here is not one of degree: on a realistic universe the sample
covariance matrix is singular, and a singular matrix does not give a noisy answer,
it gives a meaningless one.

We first set out what the optimizer is asking for and why the request cannot be
met, then work through the four available responses in order of what they cost,
then ask which of them actually pays out of sample. The answer to that last
question is less flattering than the literature on shrinkage usually suggests.

```{r}
#| label: data
cls <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)

ins <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly, date, asset, return)
eq  <- ins[, colnames(ins) %in% sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]]

c(classes = ncol(cls), equities = ncol(eq), months = nrow(cls))
```

## What the Optimizer Requires {#sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory}

A minimum-variance portfolio is the weight vector minimizing
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$ subject to the constraints,
and $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ is the entire input. Nothing else about the assets
enters: not their names, not their sectors, not their expected returns. Whatever
the matrix says about risk is risk as far as the optimizer is concerned.

Being symmetric, it holds $N(N+1)/2$ distinct numbers, estimated from $T$
observations by

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T}
  (\boldsymbol{r}_t - \bar{\boldsymbol{r}})(\boldsymbol{r}_t - \bar{\boldsymbol{r}})' .
$$ {#eq-07-sample}

Written this way the difficulty is immediate. @eq-07-sample is a sum of $T$ outer
products, each of rank one, so

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) \leq \min(N,\, T-1).
$$ {#eq-07-rank}

Whenever $N > T-1$ the estimate is singular, whatever the data look like. This is
arithmetic, not a property of markets: it would hold if the returns were coin
flips.

The sixteen asset classes of @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation need
`r ncol(cls) * (ncol(cls) + 1) / 2`. The
`r ncol(eq)` equities need
`r format(ncol(eq) * (ncol(eq) + 1) / 2, big.mark = ",")`, from
`r nrow(eq)` months of history. That asks the data to pin down more parameters
than it has observations, and at some point the answer stops being an estimate.

### What singularity claims about portfolios

@eq-07-rank is a statement about a matrix. Its consequence is a statement about
money. If $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ is singular, there exists a weight vector
$\boldsymbol{w} \neq \boldsymbol{0}$ with

$$
\boldsymbol{w}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\boldsymbol{w} = 0,
$$ {#eq-07-riskless}

a portfolio the estimate says cannot lose money, and there are as many
independent such portfolios as the matrix is short of full rank. An optimizer
told to minimize variance will find them, because that is exactly its job, and
will put everything there.

They are not real. They are long-short cancellations that happened to net out
over the particular months used for estimation, and they will not net out again.
This is the mechanism behind the familiar complaint that mean-variance
optimization produces absurd weights. @michaud1989 called the optimizer an error
maximizer for this reason, and the label is exact rather than rhetorical: among
all portfolios consistent with the constraints, the procedure selects the one the
estimate is most optimistic about, which is the one the estimate is most wrong
about.

Even short of singularity, the inverse is what the optimizer uses, and the
quantity governing how much an error in $\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ is magnified
on its way into the weights is the condition number

$$
\kappa(\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})
= \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}},
$$ {#eq-07-condition}

the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue. @laloux1999 showed that most
of the small eigenvalues of a financial correlation matrix are indistinguishable
from those of a random matrix of the same dimensions, a comparison made precise
by the limiting spectrum of @marchenko1967. The directions the optimizer most
wants to exploit are the ones carrying the least information.

@chopra1993 measured how the cost divides. Errors in expected returns hurt an
order of magnitude more than errors in variances, which in turn hurt more than
errors in covariances, which is why @sec-06-expected-returns-theory is the harder
chapter. It is also why this one is unavoidable: a singular matrix is not an
error of degree.

### Diagnosing it before the solver does

Two numbers, neither of which requires inverting anything.

```{r}
#| label: diagnose
covariance_health <- function(X) {
  S  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X))
  ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
  c(assets = ncol(X), observations = nrow(X), rank = qr(S)$rank,
    riskless_directions = sum(ev < 1e-12),
    condition = if (min(ev) <= 0) Inf else max(ev) / min(ev))
}

h_ins <- covariance_health(ins)             # all instruments, the whole sample
rbind(classes     = covariance_health(cls[1:60, ]),
      equities    = covariance_health(eq[1:60, ]),
      instruments = h_ins)
```

`rank` below `assets` means the matrix is singular, and `riskless_directions`
counts the portfolios it believes are free. Five years of data on `r ncol(eq)`
equities produces
`r covariance_health(eq[1:60, ])[["riskless_directions"]]` of them.

`condition` is the subtler warning. It is the ratio of the largest eigenvalue to
the smallest, and it bounds how much the inverse magnifies an error in the
input. A finite but very large value is more dangerous than an infinite one, because
everything still runs: the matrix inverts, weights come back, and they are a
magnified copy of the sampling noise. Past roughly $10^{8}$ the computation is
reading noise with double precision arithmetic.

The third row is that case. All `r ncol(ins)` instruments on the full
`r nrow(ins)` months have $N < T - 1$, so @eq-07-rank does not bind and every
eigenvalue is positive, yet `qr()` reports rank `r h_ins[["rank"]]` at its
default tolerance, `r h_ins[["riskless_directions"]]` eigenvalues lie below
$10^{-12}$ and the condition number is
$10^{`r sprintf("%.1f", log10(h_ins[["condition"]]))`}$. No longer sample cures
it: the cause is the bond block of @sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market,
where some instruments nearly replicate others.

```{r}
#| label: diagnose-claims
#| include: false
stopifnot(h_ins[["assets"]] < h_ins[["observations"]] - 1,
          is.finite(h_ins[["condition"]]), h_ins[["condition"]] > 1e8,
          h_ins[["rank"]] < h_ins[["assets"]], h_ins[["riskless_directions"]] > 0)
```

```{r}
#| label: rank-by-level
rank_report <- function(X, label) {
  vapply(c(60L, 120L, 180L), function(W) {
    S  <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(X[seq_len(W), ]))
    ev <- eigen(S, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
    c(T = W, N = ncol(X), rank = qr(S)$rank, min_eigen = min(ev),
      condition = if (min(ev) <= 0) Inf else max(ev) / min(ev))
  }, numeric(5)) |> t() |> as.data.frame() |> dplyr::mutate(universe = label)
}

dplyr::bind_rows(rank_report(cls, "16 classes"),
                 rank_report(eq,  "123 equities")) |>
  dplyr::select(universe, T, N, rank, min_eigen, condition)
```

Look at `min_eigen` on the two singular rows. It is **negative**. A covariance
matrix cannot have a negative eigenvalue; that is floating-point noise around an
eigenvalue which is exactly zero. The matrix is not imprecise. It describes a
world in which some portfolio has negative variance.

### Why this book has not needed the chapter until now

Every allocation up to here happened across asset classes, and at that level the
problem does not arise.

```{r}
#| label: windows-invertible
bad <- sum(vapply(seq.int(61L, nrow(cls)), function(i) {
  qr(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[(i - 60L):(i - 1L), ])))$rank < ncol(cls)
}, logical(1)))

c(rolling_windows = nrow(cls) - 60L, rank_deficient = bad)
```

Not one sixty-month window in the sample is rank deficient at class level.
The moment @sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory descends into individual securities it
becomes the only question that matters, and nothing about the data has changed.
What changed is how many things the portfolio was asked to hold.

## Four Routes {#sec-07-covariance-matrix-implementation}

There are four routes. Two change what may be owned, two change how it is
estimated. We take them in order of what they cost.

### Route one: hold fewer things

The cheapest fix is not to have the problem. Allocating across sixteen classes
rather than `r ncol(eq)` securities, or across sector sleeves rather than names,
leaves a matrix comfortably estimable on five years.

This is not a dodge. Most institutional mandates are set at exactly this level
for exactly this reason, and @sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory treats the sleeve structure
as a decision rather than a convenience. It does not help when the mandate names `r ncol(eq)` securities, which is what a
stock selection process hands its allocator.

### Route two: impose a structure

If `r format(ncol(eq) * (ncol(eq) + 1) / 2, big.mark = ",")` free parameters
cannot be estimated, the answer is to stop trying to. Assert instead that returns
are driven by $k$ common factors plus asset-specific noise, so that

$$
\boldsymbol{r}_t = \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{f}_t + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_t,
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{\Omega}\boldsymbol{B}' + \boldsymbol{D},
$$ {#eq-07-factor}

with $\boldsymbol{B}$ the $N \times k$ loadings, $\boldsymbol{\Omega}$ the
covariance of the factors and $\boldsymbol{D}$ a diagonal matrix of residual
variances. That is $Nk + N$ numbers rather than $N(N+1)/2$: for three factors on
`r ncol(eq)` assets, `r ncol(eq) * 3 + ncol(eq)` rather than several thousand.
Because $\boldsymbol{D}$ is positive by construction, @eq-07-factor cannot be
singular whatever $T$ is. @fan2008 give the conditions under which it converges
where @eq-07-sample does not, and @bai2002 and @connor1993 the machinery for
choosing $k$ rather than asserting it.

The factors can be economic, as in @sec-05-factor-models-implementation, or
purely statistical, the principal components of the returns themselves. The
second is six lines.

```{r}
#| label: factor-covariance
factor_covariance <- function(X, k = 3L) {
  x  <- zoo::coredata(X)
  pc <- prcomp(x)
  B  <- pc$rotation[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE]      # loadings, N x k
  f  <- x %*% B                                      # factor realizations
  e  <- x - f %*% t(B)                               # residuals
  e  <- sweep(e, 2, colMeans(e))
  B %*% stats::cov(f) %*% t(B) + diag(colSums(e^2) / (nrow(x) - k - 1L))
}

S_fac <- factor_covariance(eq[1:120, ], k = 3L)
e_fac <- eigen(S_fac, symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
c(rank = qr(S_fac)$rank, min_eigen = min(e_fac),
  condition = max(e_fac) / min(e_fac))
```

Full rank on a window where the sample matrix has
`r covariance_health(eq[1:120, ])[["riskless_directions"]]` riskless directions,
and a condition number of `r sprintf("%.0f", max(e_fac) / min(e_fac))` where the
sample matrix's is infinite. The structure does the work: because every asset's risk runs through three
shared factors, no combination can cancel to zero unless the residuals do, and
those are positive by construction.

`PortfolioAnalytics` ships this as `statistical.factor.model()`, with one
constraint worth knowing about in the released version.

```{r}
#| label: factor-model-package
sapply(c(60L, 120L, 180L), function(W) {
  tryCatch({ statistical.factor.model(eq[seq_len(W), ], k = 3L); "accepted" },
           error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
})
```

It requires at least as many observations as assets, which is precisely the
condition under which it is not needed. The body of the function does not:
principal components need enough components, not enough columns, which is why the
six lines above run on the same window. @sec-93-package-notes records the patch that relaxes the check and
where it stands.

### Route three: shrink the matrix

Keep every asset and keep the sample estimate, but pull it part of the way
towards a target that is well conditioned by construction:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\text{shrunk}}
= (1-\lambda)\,\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}} + \lambda\,\boldsymbol{F},
\qquad \lambda \in [0, 1],
$$ {#eq-07-shrinkage}

with $\boldsymbol{F}$ commonly a scaled identity and sometimes a
constant-correlation or factor matrix. The construction descends from @stein1956,
who showed that shrinking a multivariate estimate towards a fixed point can
dominate the sample estimate in mean squared error despite being biased.
@ledoit2003 and @ledoit2004 derive the $\lambda$ minimizing expected loss and
show that it can be estimated from the data, so it is not a tuning parameter
anyone has to guess; @schafer2005 give the analytic form `corpcor` implements,
and @ledoit2017 extend it to shrink each eigenvalue by a different amount.

This is the workhorse. It needs no assumption about what drives returns, it
cannot fail, and @eq-07-shrinkage is invertible whenever $\boldsymbol{F}$ is and
$\lambda > 0$.

```{r}
#| label: shrunk
S_shr <- corpcor::cov.shrink(zoo::coredata(eq[1:120, ]), verbose = FALSE)
c(lambda = attr(S_shr, "lambda"),
  rank = qr(S_shr)$rank,
  min_eigen = min(eigen(as.matrix(S_shr), symmetric = TRUE,
                        only.values = TRUE)$values))
```

`lambda` is the weight on the target rather than on the data,
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * attr(S_shr, "lambda"))` of the way towards
independence here.

### Route four: estimate robustly

The three routes above address a matrix badly conditioned because the sample is
short. A robust estimator addresses one badly centered because a few observations
dominate it. That is a different problem, and it is taken up below.

### Getting any of this into the optimizer

`PortfolioAnalytics` routes every moment estimate through one function, and the
released version of that function does not offer shrinkage.

```{r}
#| label: moment-methods
eval(formals(set.portfolio.moments)$method)
```

`sample` is the sample matrix, `boudt` a factor-based cleaning of the higher
moments, `black_litterman` and `meucci` view-blending machinery belonging in
@sec-17-expressing-views-theory. None of them is route three.

This is the point at which many users give up and compute weights outside the
package, discarding every constraint and diagnostic it provides. That is
unnecessary. `optimize.portfolio()` takes a `momentFUN` argument, and it accepts
a function object rather than merely the name of one.

```{r}
#| label: momentfun-takes-a-function
shrinkage_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  X <- zoo::coredata(R)
  S <- corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE)
  S <- matrix(as.numeric(S), ncol(X), ncol(X),
              dimnames = list(colnames(X), colnames(X)))
  list(mu = colMeans(X), sigma = S, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL,
       mean = colMeans(X), var = S)
}

spec <- portfolio.spec(colnames(eq)) |>
  add.constraint("full_investment") |> add.constraint("long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var")

opt <- optimize.portfolio(eq[1:120, ], spec, optimize_method = "ROI",
                          momentFUN = shrinkage_moments)
w <- extractWeights(opt)
c(holdings = sum(w > 1e-6), sum = sum(w), max_weight = max(w))
```

Because it is a function rather than a name, it can be built on the fly with its
settings baked in: one per shrinkage intensity to be compared, or one closing over
a factor model fitted elsewhere. Nothing has to live in the global environment.

::: {.callout-important}
## A moment function must set both pairs of names

The returned list carries `mu` and `sigma`, and also `mean` and `var`. Different
code paths inside the package read different names, so a moment function that
sets only one pair works until the objective changes and then fails in a way that
points nowhere near the cause. The matrix must also be a plain `matrix` carrying
dimnames, because `cov.shrink()` returns attributes that some downstream code
does not expect.
:::

### When the package function is the thing in the way

There is a third option beyond using a function and working around it, and on an
open source package it is usually the right one: fix it and send the fix back.
The constraint in `statistical.factor.model()` is one line, the reason it is
wrong is demonstrable in a paragraph, and a patch with a test is less work than
the workaround it replaces. @sec-93-package-notes lists the patches this book
contributed and their state, which is also the only honest way to tell a reader
which behavior to expect.

### Route four in full: robust estimation

`PortfolioAnalytics` ships a family of robust covariance estimators that almost
nobody uses and that no textbook of this generation covers.

```{r}
#| label: robust-family
grep("covRob", ls("package:PortfolioAnalytics"), value = TRUE)
```

These answer route four. Shrinkage repairs a matrix badly conditioned because the
sample is short; a robust estimator repairs one badly centered because a few
months dominate it, whether a flash crash, a redenomination or a bad print in a
vendor file. The minimum covariance determinant estimator behind
`custom.covRob.Mcd()` searches for the subset of $h$ observations whose sample
covariance has the smallest determinant and estimates from that subset alone,
discarding the rest [@rousseeuw1984; @rousseeuw1999].

They plug in exactly where route three did.

```{r}
#| label: robust-demo
robust_moments <- function(R, portfolio) {
  m <- custom.covRob.Mcd(zoo::coredata(R))
  list(mu = m$mu, sigma = m$sigma, m3 = NULL, m4 = NULL,
       mean = m$mu, var = m$sigma)
}

rb <- robust_moments(cls[1:120, ])
sb <- stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[1:120, ]))
c(robust_mean_vol = mean(sqrt(diag(rb$sigma))) * sqrt(12),
  sample_mean_vol = mean(sqrt(diag(sb))) * sqrt(12))
```

The robust estimate of volatility is lower, because it has judged part of what
the sample matrix calls risk to be a few unusual months rather than the process.
Whether that is an improvement is a judgment about the world rather than about
the estimator: right if those months were contamination, wrong if they were the
tail an investor is paid to bear. @sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application found
that this market's extreme months arrive together across series, which argues for
the second reading. @sec-28-robustness-theory makes the
case properly, and @sec-10-risk-measures-theory is where discarding the tail
stops being defensible.

## What the Routes Do to the Matrix {#sec-07-covariance-matrix-application}

### Scoring the routes out of sample

This is not a question the matrix can answer. Every estimator reports a
flattering number about itself in sample. The only honest test is to estimate on
one window, hold the resulting portfolio for a month, and score what happened.

`R/ch05-estimator-race.R` does that for four estimators and three window lengths,
long only and fully invested, rebalanced monthly. All three windows are scored on
the same months, so a longer window earns no credit for starting later.

```{r}
#| label: equal-weight-control
FIRST_OOS <- 181L
oos    <- seq.int(FIRST_OOS, nrow(eq))
stopifnot(all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == zoo::index(eq)))   # the bill lines up
ew_ret <- rowMeans(zoo::coredata(eq[oos, ]))
ew_ex  <- ew_ret - sim_riskfree_monthly$return[oos]

ew <- c(ann_vol = stats::sd(ew_ret) * sqrt(12),
        ann_ret = mean(ew_ret) * 12,
        sharpe  = mean(ew_ex) / stats::sd(ew_ex) * sqrt(12))
round(ew, 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-07-race
#| tbl-cap: "Minimum variance on 123 equities, scored out of sample on identical months. `failed` counts the rebalancing dates that produced no portfolio at all."
#| echo: false
race <- readRDS("output/tables/ch05-estimator-race.rds")
race |>
  dplyr::transmute(window, estimator,
                   failed = sprintf("%d of %d", failed, periods),
                   ann_vol, sharpe, eff_bets, lambda) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 4, 3, 1, 3))
```

```{r}
#| label: race-claims
#| include: false
# Every order and sign the reading of the race states.
at   <- function(est, W, col) race[[col]][race$estimator == est & race$window == W]
r180 <- race[race$window == 180, ]
dies <- race$estimator %in% c("sample", "factor3") & race$window < 180
stopifnot(
  all(race$failed[dies] == race$periods[1]), all(race$failed[!dies] == 0),
  at("shrunk", 60, "ann_vol") < at("diagonal", 60, "ann_vol"),
  at("shrunk", 120, "ann_vol") < at("diagonal", 120, "ann_vol"),
  at("diagonal", 120, "ann_vol") < ew[["ann_vol"]],
  abs(at("shrunk", 180, "ann_vol") - at("sample", 180, "ann_vol")) < 0.001,
  at("factor3", 180, "ann_vol") > max(r180$ann_vol[r180$estimator %in% c("sample", "shrunk")]),
  at("factor3", 180, "sharpe") < min(r180$sharpe[r180$estimator %in% c("sample", "shrunk")]),
  diff(race$lambda[race$estimator == "shrunk"]) < 0,
  which.min(r180$ann_vol) != which.max(r180$sharpe),
  at("shrunk", 120, "sharpe") > ew[["sharpe"]], at("shrunk", 120, "ann_ret") < ew[["ann_ret"]]
)
```

Read `failed` first. At sixty and at one hundred and twenty months, two of the
four estimators produce nothing at all, not a poor portfolio but no portfolio, on
every one of the `r race$periods[1]` rebalancing dates. That is @eq-07-rank
arriving as an empty result. Route three and the diagonal target reach a weight
vector; the sample matrix and the released factor model do not.

Where the sample matrix fails, shrinkage gives the lower volatility of the two
estimators that run:
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * race$ann_vol[race$estimator == "shrunk" & race$window == 120])`
at a hundred and twenty months against
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * race$ann_vol[race$estimator == "diagonal" & race$window == 120])`
for the diagonal and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ew[["ann_vol"]])` for holding everything equally.

Then the row that keeps this from being an advertisement.

```{r}
#| label: the-tie
#| echo: false
race |>
  dplyr::filter(window == 180) |>
  dplyr::select(estimator, ann_vol, sharpe, lambda) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 4, 3, 3))
```

At a hundred and eighty months the sample matrix is finally estimable and
shrinkage stops buying anything:
`r sprintf("%.4f", race$ann_vol[race$estimator == "shrunk" & race$window == 180])`
against
`r sprintf("%.4f", race$ann_vol[race$estimator == "sample" & race$window == 180])`
is a dead heat, and the factor model is marginally behind both on volatility
and further behind on Sharpe ratio. Shrinkage is
not a better estimator in general. It is the estimator that exists when the
others do not, which is a different and more useful property.

The `lambda` column says so from the inside: it falls from
`r sprintf("%.3f", race$lambda[race$estimator == "shrunk" & race$window == 60])`
to
`r sprintf("%.3f", race$lambda[race$estimator == "shrunk" & race$window == 180])`
as the window lengthens. The procedure asks for less help as it needs less, which
is the practical content of the Ledoit-Wolf result.

### Lower volatility is not a better portfolio

`sharpe` is not `ann_vol`, and the ordering is not the same. At a hundred and
eighty months the sample matrix has the lowest volatility and shrinkage the
highest Sharpe ratio, and the factor model, within a tenth of a point of both on
volatility, trails them by
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(r180$sharpe[r180$estimator %in% c("sample", "shrunk")]) - at("factor3", 180, "sharpe"))`
on Sharpe ratio. Volatility was the objective, and it does not rank the results.

Minimum variance did what it was asked. It cut annualized volatility from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ew[["ann_vol"]])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * at("shrunk", 120, "ann_vol"))`,
about a third, and gave up
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (ew[["ann_ret"]] - at("shrunk", 120, "ann_ret")))`
percentage points of annual return for it, so on this market it finished ahead
of equal weighting on Sharpe ratio as well,
`r sprintf("%.3f", at("shrunk", 120, "sharpe"))` against
`r sprintf("%.3f", ew[["sharpe"]])`. That is not the general finding:
@demiguel2009 report that across their universes no optimized rule, minimum
variance included, is reliably ahead of equal weighting, and whether the
advantage here belongs to the method or to this sample is the subject of
@sec-08-estimation-error-theory.

Every route is one operation on the eigenvalues of @eq-07-sample, and it is
easier to see than to derive.

```{r}
#| label: spectrum
X   <- zoo::coredata(eq[1:120, ])
ev  <- function(S) pmax(eigen(as.matrix(S), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values, 0)
e_s <- ev(stats::cov(X))
e_h <- ev(corpcor::cov.shrink(X, verbose = FALSE))

tibble::tibble(
  matrix      = c("sample", "shrunk"),
  largest     = c(e_s[1], e_h[1]),
  smallest    = c(min(e_s), min(e_h)),
  zero_eigens = c(sum(e_s < 1e-12), sum(e_h < 1e-12)),
  condition   = c(e_s[1] / max(min(e_s), .Machine$double.eps), e_h[1] / min(e_h)))
```

`r sum(e_s < 1e-12)` eigenvalues of the sample matrix are zero. Those are the
riskless portfolios of @eq-07-riskless seen from the other side, and they are not
a property of these particular equities. They would be there if the returns were
coin flips, because `r nrow(X)` observations cannot pin down `r ncol(X)`
directions, by @eq-07-rank.

```{r}
#| label: fig-07-spectrum
#| fig-cap: "The eigenvalue spectrum before and after shrinkage, on a log scale. The sample matrix runs off the bottom of the plot: several of its eigenvalues are exactly zero. Shrinkage compresses the range from fifteen orders of magnitude to two."
#| echo: false
spec_df <- rbind(
  data.frame(i = seq_along(e_s), value = pmax(e_s, 1e-20), matrix = "sample"),
  data.frame(i = seq_along(e_h), value = e_h,              matrix = "shrunk"))

ggplot2::ggplot(spec_df, ggplot2::aes(i, value, colour = matrix)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_log10() +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = unname(tidyaa_colors[c("ink", "caution")]),
                               name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1e-8, NA)) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "eigenvalue, largest to smallest", y = "value (log scale)")
```

The largest falls by `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - e_h[1] / e_s[1]))` and the
smallest non-zero one rises by a factor of
`r sprintf("%.0f", min(e_h) / min(e_s[e_s > 1e-12]))`, which is @eq-07-condition
brought back into a range where the inverse means something. That is what a
shrinkage target is: not a better guess at any individual covariance, but a
statement that the extremes of a sample spectrum are mostly sampling error and
belong nearer the middle, which is the reading @laloux1999 gave them. A factor
model reaches the same place by another road, building @eq-07-factor from a few
directions plus a positive residual for every asset, so that small eigenvalues
cannot be zero to begin with.

### Shrink towards what, when the target moves?

The usual $\boldsymbol{F}$ in @eq-07-shrinkage is a scaled identity: equal
variances, no correlations. It is chosen for being maximally unlike the noisy
thing it corrects, not for being true. How untrue it is depends on when the
question is asked.

```{r}
#| label: regimes
d      <- zoo::index(cls)
in_ep  <- vapply(sim_episodes$episode, function(e) in_episode(d, e),
                 logical(length(d)))
crisis <- in_ep[, "credit_crisis"]
calm   <- rowSums(in_ep) == 0               # outside all four episodes

regime_shape <- function(keep) {
  e <- ev(stats::cov(zoo::coredata(cls[keep, ])))
  C <- stats::cor(cls[keep, ])
  data.frame(months = sum(keep), pc1_share = e[1] / sum(e),
             directions = sum(e)^2 / sum(e^2),
             mean_correlation = mean(C[upper.tri(C)]))
}

# A short sample concentrates its spectrum whatever the market does, so score
# every run of calm months of the crisis's length as well.
n_c   <- sum(crisis)
runs  <- which(vapply(seq_len(length(d) - n_c + 1L),
                      function(i) all(calm[i + seq_len(n_c) - 1L]), logical(1)))
short <- do.call(rbind, lapply(runs, function(i) {
  regime_shape(seq_along(d) %in% (i + seq_len(n_c) - 1L))
}))

shape <- rbind(calm       = regime_shape(calm),
               calm_short = as.data.frame(lapply(short, stats::median)),
               crisis     = regime_shape(crisis))
shape$regime <- rownames(shape)
shape[, c("regime", "months", "pc1_share", "directions", "mean_correlation")]
```

```{r}
#| label: regimes-claims
#| include: false
# The signs the reading rests on, and how far the crisis lies outside the calm
# windows of its own length.
beyond <- c(pc1 = mean(short$pc1_share < shape["crisis", "pc1_share"]),
            cor = mean(short$mean_correlation < shape["crisis", "mean_correlation"]))
stopifnot(
  n_c < ncol(cls), nrow(short) > 100, beyond > 0.9,
  diff(shape$pc1_share) > 0, diff(shape$directions) < 0,
  shape["crisis", "mean_correlation"] > shape["calm", "mean_correlation"],
  abs(diff(shape$mean_correlation[1:2])) < 0.05
)
```

The calm sample is the `r shape["calm", "months"]` months outside the four
episodes of `sim_episodes`, the crisis the `r n_c` months of the credit crisis.
In calm months the first principal component carries
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * shape["calm", "pc1_share"])` of the variance and the
matrix behaves like roughly `r sprintf("%.1f", shape["calm", "directions"])`
independent directions; through the credit crisis the same sixteen series carry
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * shape["crisis", "pc1_share"])` and collapse to
`r sprintf("%.1f", shape["crisis", "directions"])`. Part of that is arithmetic,
since by @eq-07-rank a `r n_c`-month matrix has at most `r n_c - 1` non-zero
eigenvalues and the median calm window of that length already shows
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * shape["calm_short", "pc1_share"])` and
`r sprintf("%.1f", shape["calm_short", "directions"])`, but the crisis lies
beyond `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * beyond[["pc1"]])` of those windows, and
average pairwise correlation, which no rank bound touches, rises from
`r sprintf("%.2f", shape["calm", "mean_correlation"])` to
`r sprintf("%.2f", shape["crisis", "mean_correlation"])`, above
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * beyond[["cor"]])` of them.

A diagonal target asserts that the assets are unrelated. In calm months that is
wrong by some margin; in the credit crisis it is wrong by far more, and precisely
when the portfolio depends on it. Shrinking towards independence is least defensible
exactly when it does the most work, which is the honest reason to prefer a factor
target where one is available. @sec-19-regimes-theory is where this choice stops
being a footnote.

### The shrinkage already in place

One last connection, because it reframes much of this book. Every optimization so
far has been long only. @jagannathan2003 showed that a non-negativity constraint
is not merely a restriction: it acts on the solution the way @eq-07-shrinkage acts
on the matrix, because it forbids exactly the large offsetting long-short
positions that @eq-07-riskless invites. Their finding is that imposing the
constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when it is known to be false, which is
why a constrained optimization on a sample matrix behaves far better than the
unconstrained arithmetic suggests. @frost1988 reach the same conclusion from the
Bayesian side.

That is worth holding next to @tbl-07-race. Route three took about a third off
the volatility of an equal-weighted sleeve. The long-only constraint, imposed for
reasons of mandate rather than of statistics, had already done a comparable amount
of work for nothing.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- By @eq-07-rank the sample covariance matrix is singular whenever there are more
  assets than observations, regardless of the data. On 123 equities and five
  years of monthly returns it is short of full rank by more than sixty.
- A singular estimate does not merely give a noisy answer. By @eq-07-riskless it
  asserts that some portfolio has zero variance, and a minimizer will find it and
  hold it.
- Even without singularity, the condition number of @eq-07-condition measures how
  much an input error is magnified in the weights, and the smallest eigenvalues
  of a financial covariance matrix are largely indistinguishable from noise
  [@laloux1999; @marchenko1967].
- There are four responses: hold fewer assets, impose the factor structure of
  @eq-07-factor, shrink towards a well-conditioned target as in
  @eq-07-shrinkage, or estimate robustly. The first three address conditioning;
  the fourth addresses contamination, which is a different complaint.
- Shrinkage is not a better estimator in general. Scored out of sample it wins
  where the sample matrix cannot be computed at all, and ties with it once the
  window is long enough. Its own $\lambda$ falls as the window grows, which is
  the procedure reporting that it is needed less.
- Minimum variance did what it was asked and cut volatility by about a third,
  and on this market it finished ahead of equal weighting on Sharpe ratio as
  well. Whether that survives on other universes is
  @sec-08-estimation-error-theory's subject.
- The long-only constraint is itself a form of shrinkage and was already doing
  comparable work before any estimator was changed [@jagannathan2003].

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Apply `covariance_health()` to the government and credit instruments of
   `sim_assets` alone, on the full sample. There are far more observations than
   assets, so @eq-07-rank does not bind, and the matrix is nearly singular all
   the same. Identify the reason from the eigenvectors of the smallest
   eigenvalues rather than from the asset names.
2. `corpcor::cov.shrink()` chooses `lambda` analytically. Fix it instead at
   0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 and plot realized out-of-sample volatility against it.
   Where is the minimum, and is the analytic choice near it?
3. Replace `shrinkage_moments()` with one built on `factor_covariance()` and
   compare them on the same rolling windows. At which window length does the
   factor structure stop helping, and does that coincide with the point where the
   sample matrix becomes estimable?
4. Repeat the unconstrained minimum-variance optimization of
   @sec-09-mean-variance-theory on the `r ncol(eq)` equities with the shrunk
   matrix, once long only and once with weights free to go negative. Quantify the
   @jagannathan2003 effect on this data.
